item.title: Snap Layouts wasn't built for ultrawide monitors, so I built my own with PowerToys
item.itunes:title: Snap Layouts wasn't built for ultrawide monitors, so I built my own with PowerToys
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've used the Alienware AW3423DW OLED for the last four years, and though I bought it for gaming, I now mostly use it as a secondary monitor that gives me plenty of room to multitask. That 21:9 aspect ratio gives me extra width to keep multiple windows open side by side without making any of them feel too cramped. And since I'm usually juggling Discord, Chrome, and TradingView, even while gaming, Snap Layouts were a no-brainer for quickly organizing everything.

Now, as much as I've enjoyed using Snap Layouts since Windows 11 first launched, I've always found the preset layouts a little too restrictive for an ultrawide monitor. Even though Microsoft says the layouts you see may depend on display size, my ultrawide doesn't get anything particularly special compared to my other two 16:9 monitors. That's what convinced me to try out FancyZones in Microsoft PowerToys when I first read about it, and after seeing how much more customizable it is, I haven't looked back.

4 Windows 11 tiling managers that put Microsoft’s Snap Layouts to shame

Upgrade your productivity

1
By  João Carrasqueira

FancyZones lets me build the layout I want

And I can have a different layout for each of my three monitors

If you just use FancyZones as it is after installing PowerToys, you're going to be disappointed because you only have like five preset layouts to choose from. Snap Layouts, on the other hand, gives me eight on each monitor. So, to take full advantage of it, you need to create a custom layout by going to PowerToys Settings -> FancyZones -> Open layout editor. Since my main issue with Snap Layouts was that it didn't give me a layout to arrange four windows horizontally, that's exactly what I created.

I split my ultrawide into four equal zones, and now I can fit four windows side by side without having to manually resize each one afterward. You can go crazy with the layouts, but I just wanted something practical. My favorite part about FancyZones is that it remembers which layout I've assigned to each monitor. For my 4K monitor, I created the same four-window grid that I'm used to with Snap Layouts, and for my other standard 1440p one, I created a simple two-column layout. This way, each of my three monitors has a layout that actually suits how I use it.

FancyZones gets the snapping part right

I don't have to drag windows all the way to the edges

For a feature called "Snap Layouts," you'd expect the actual snapping process to be its biggest strength. Except it's only straightforward when you're snapping windows to the edges or corners of your screen. To see more layout options, you need to drag a window all the way to the top edge of your monitor. And then you still have to drop the window into the zone you want. Of course, you can hover over the maximize button instead, but even that's near the top-right corner, so you're still mostly moving your cursor across the screen just to bring up the layouts.

With FancyZones, I just hold Shift while dragging a window, and my custom zones immediately show up. Then I can drop the window into whichever zone I want without dragging it to the top edge of my screen first. This might not seem like a big deal, but on a 34-inch ultrawide, it saves me a lot of mouse movement when I'm constantly rearranging windows. And since I already know where each zone is, I don't have to stop and think about where I want to put the window every time.

Snap Layouts has simplicity going for it, though

But FancyZones is mostly a one-time setup that only takes a few minutes

If there's one thing Snap Layouts gets right, it's that you don't have to set anything up. If you like the predefined layouts, you don't need to mess around with anything else. And if you just want a simple split-screen or four windows arranged in a grid, you don't even need to bring up the layouts in the first place. The layout you want to use can change depending on what you're doing, too, and Snap Layouts makes it easy to switch between them on the fly. With FancyZones, it's not nearly as straightforward until you set it up properly.

But you only need to set it up the way you like once. For instance, you can create multiple custom layouts and assign a number to each of them. After that, you can switch between them any time by pressing Win + Ctrl + Alt + [number]. The keybind is kind of ridiculous, but I've rarely found myself needing to switch layouts on my ultrawide anyway. And I can still use Snap Layouts when I want a different arrangement. So I can basically use whichever one makes more sense at the time, depending on whether I'm holding that Shift key when I drag a window around.

Snap Layouts needs more customization to win me back

I don't think it should be hard for Microsoft to add a few more layout options to Snap Layouts. Even something as simple as letting me arrange four windows horizontally would solve my biggest problem with it on an ultrawide. But ideally, I'd like to see Microsoft go a step further and let me create my own layouts. And the whole snapping process could use some work, too. After using FancyZones, I now prefer holding another key to have my zones appear while dragging a window. Maybe one day we'll get that flexibility in Snap Layouts, but until then, I'm keeping FancyZones enabled alongside the other PowerToys utilities I now use every day.

item.itunes:summary:
This UGREEN DXP4800 Plus NAS is perfect for beginners and suitable for advanced users. The $730 price tag is steep, but the Amazon discount that knocks 20% off makes it easier on the wallet. The UGREEN DXP4800 Plus is still pricey, but this is the lowest price we've seen in quite some time.

The Ugreen DXP4800 Plus is a NAS that runs the company's own UGOS, and it comes with an Intel Pentium 8505, 8GB of RAM, and up to four drive bays.

Those that are deep into NAS builds will never be satisfied with what's on the shelves. The ability to endlessly customize can become a bit of a rabbit hole if you're not careful. But for most people, this UGREEN NAS is going to be the perfect device to back up all your information.

The UGOS Pro software might not be perfect, but the brand does make it easy to get started. Plus, it's always updating the software so that it offers more features, making it easier for everyone to use. It offers an easy-to-understand interface, and you can start hosting your information with just a few clicks.

Download the corresponding app on your devices, and you can easily access the NAS from anywhere, so long as you have a internet connection. This model is a 4-bay device, which means you can install up to four drives, expanding the storage to 144TB. The device is also quite quick and versatile thanks to its Intel processor paired with 8GB of RAM.

Transfer speeds are quite quick too, with dual Ethernet, with 10Gb and 2.5Gb ports. And just in case you want to expand the capabilities, you can install different operating systems and software. The NAS has a 128GB SSD that allows for ample expansion. Again, starting out, UGOS Pro is more than enough. But you can also install something like TrueNAS Scale if you want.

item.title: Flathub just reversed its AI-generated content ban, but developers still need to say they used it
item.itunes:title: Flathub just reversed its AI-generated content ban, but developers still need to say they used it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Flathub now allows AI-generated code if disclosed and labeled with the affected parts and extent.
  • Submitters must be human; agents can't generate commits, descriptions, reviews, or replies.
  • Maintainers can still reject AI-labeled or fully vibe-coded apps if they are low quality or problematic.

Back in May of this year, we reported that Flathub banned AI-generated submissions because people were being a little rude about it.

Now, as more and more Linux distros have declared acceptance of LLM-created code (as long as it's of high quality, of course), it seems that Flathub has had a change of heart. Fortunately, while the new rules allow AI content if it's properly disclosed, they don't open the door for people to flood the repository with poorly made apps.

Flathub now allows AI-generated apps, but they still have to be good

People can't get out of submitting bad apps just because they said an AI made it

As spotted by Linuxiac, Flathub has gone back on its ban on LLM-created content. Now, in a revised commit to the documentation, the rules begin as follows:

Submitters must disclose any AI-generated code, documentation, packaging, or other material they know or reasonably believe is included in the application or its Flathub packaging. The disclosure must identify the affected parts and approximate extent.

This doesn't mean someone can tell an LLM to make an app in five minutes, slap a disclosure on it, submit it, and earn immunity from being taken off Flathub. If the maintainers believe a project was entirely vibe-coded, or they have "concerns about its review, quality,

or maintainability," they can reject an app even if the submitter correctly labeled their work. It seems like a push to encourage AI tools without opening the door to a tidal wave of vibe-coded apps that overwhelm maintainers.

On top of that, people cannot just spin up an AI agent and have it maintain their project for them. Humans must submit the work themselves, and an agent cannot "generate their commit messages, descriptions, review comments, or replies." This is likely to stop people from parking an agent on a project and having it do all the maintenance work.

Linus Torvalds used AI to fix a Linux bug, and now LLM critics on Linux face an uncomfortable choice

Avoiding software without AI code is getting very difficult.

27

item.title: The most useful productivity tool I installed this year costs nothing and does one thing perfectly
item.itunes:title: The most useful productivity tool I installed this year costs nothing and does one thing perfectly
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I’ve installed plenty of productivity apps over the years, and most of them promise to help me work faster, stay organized, or save time. This year, though, the app that made the biggest difference was one I almost overlooked. It isn’t a task manager, note-taking app, or AI assistant. It’s a small Windows utility that sits quietly in the background and solves a problem I didn’t realize was slowing me down. After using it regularly, I started wondering how something this simple had become one of the most useful tools in my workflow.

Windows clipboard history wasn’t enough

I needed more from my clipboard

Windows' built-in clipboard history was useful, but I kept hitting its limits. I could press Win + V and see a few recent items, which was enough for basic tasks. But as my work became more detailed, I noticed how quickly that history became hard to use.

item.title: AMD squeezed a lightweight FSR 4 model onto handhelds, but older devices might miss out
item.itunes:title: AMD squeezed a lightweight FSR 4 model onto handhelds, but older devices might miss out
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • AMD will bring a lightweight FSR 4 to APUs, gaming laptops, and handhelds by the end of the year (pre‑2027).
  • Lightweight FSR 4 could fit older handhelds, but AMD hasn't confirmed updates to existing devices.
  • AMD will expand FSR 4 across existing APUs and new product lines; exact rollout details remain unclear.

Back when AMD brought FSR 4 to GPUs (including retroactively adding it to older models), AMD said it was a little skeptical about squeezing the same tech onto handhelds. It never explicitly stated it would never bring FSR 4 to devices such as handhelds, but it never outright confirmed that it would, either.

Now, AMD has announced a new lightweight version of FSR 4 for handheld APUs, and while it sounds like the tech may now be small enough to fit on older handhelds, we still don't know for sure if AMD can, or will, bring the tech to existing handhelds.

AMD's FSR 4 will arrive on "APUs, gaming laptops, and handheld devices" before 2027

It may just be new models that will get it, though

As spotted by The Verge, South Korean publications such as TheElec reported that Jack Huynh, the Senior Vice President and General Manager of AMD’s Computing and Graphics Group, spoke at Seoul Dragon City in Yongsan. During the meeting, Huynh said the following (machine-translated from Korean):

"We will expand the machine learning AI-based FSR4 technology, which was first introduced to existing external graphics cards, to the entire product line, including APUs, gaming laptops, and handheld devices, by the end of this year. We plan to respond in two directions: launching existing APUs and new product lines."

To achieve this, AMD will release a lightweight version of FSR 4 designed to run off APUs. But if the company is going that far, could it add FSR 4 to older hardware, as it did with GPUs? Unfortunately, Huynh neither confirmed nor denied this would happen; just that we'll see something before 2027 comes around. Maybe it's only for new devices, or maybe not; either way, we've reached out to AMD for context, so stay tuned.

item.title: I drove 10,000 miles with Google Maps, and found 6 hidden features actually worth using
item.itunes:title: I drove 10,000 miles with Google Maps, and found 6 hidden features actually worth using
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
After driving about 10,000 miles with Google Maps on my phone and Android Auto, I have figured out which tools genuinely make a difference and which I can happily ignore. A few of my favorites are buried deep in menus, while others are right in front of you but easy to overlook.

These are the Google Maps features that actually earned a permanent place in my driving routine.

Add your favorite routes to the home screen

Put frequent routes one tap away

One Google Maps feature I rarely see people talk about is adding frequently used directions directly to the Android home screen. I use this for destinations I drive to regularly, since it saves me from opening Maps, searching for the place, tapping directions, and setting everything up again.

When you start directions in Google Maps, tap the three-dot icon in the top-right corner and select Add route to Home screen. I can also set transportation mode and preferences, like avoiding tolls. Once I save it to my home screen, a single tap takes me straight into Maps with directions ready to go.

I like this for places that aren’t my Home or Work address, but that I still visit often. I can keep a few of these shortcuts inside a folder, so my most common routes are ready to go.

Set depart or arrive time

Plan the drive before leaving home

This is one of those Google Maps features I ignored for far too long. Instead of checking a route only when I am about to leave, I can tell Maps when I plan to depart or when I need to arrive. It then gives me an estimated travel time based on typical traffic conditions around that period.

I use the Arrive by option more often. If I have a hotel check-in at 3pm, a meeting at noon, or an appointment across town, I enter the arrival time and let Maps work backward to show when I should leave. The Depart at option is equally useful when I am planning a trip for a few hours or even days in advance. The option is available under the same three-dot menu in Directions.

Enable built-in speedometer

Keep your speed in plain sight

I like having Google Maps built-in speedometer enabled because it keeps one more useful piece of information right inside the navigation screen. Maps shows my current driving speed in the corner, so I don’t have to glance between the Android Auto display and the car’s instrument cluster as often.

In supported areas, Maps can also show the posted speed limit, which makes the feature even more useful on unfamiliar roads.

Changing the vehicle engine type actually helps

Tell Maps what you actually drive

Google Maps lets me specify whether I drive a petrol, diesel, hybrid, or electric vehicle, and it uses that information when suggesting fuel-efficient routes.

Since I drive a petrol car, I've configured Maps accordingly. It sounds like a minor preference, but it can influence which route Maps highlights when two options have similar arrival times. While you are in the Settings > Your Vehicles menu, make sure to change the driving avatar as well.

Look for routes that offer similar or slightly longer ETAs

The fastest route isn’t always the best

After driving thousands of miles, I rarely hit Start the moment Google Maps generates a route. Instead, I look at the alternative routes displayed alongside the recommended one.

Sometimes Maps suggests one route that takes 48 minutes while another takes 52 minutes. In that situation, I inspect both before deciding. The slightly longer route might keep me on a major highway, involve fewer turns, or simply look easier to drive. I now tap each alternative route to compare it before starting navigation. Saving two or three minutes isn’t always worth taking a route that looks more complicated.

Use Gemini with Google Maps

Let Gemini handle Maps hands-free

Gemini has made Google Maps much more useful for me because I can control several navigation functions without digging through menus. While navigating, I can ask Gemini to show alternative routes, add a stop, send my ETA to my wife on Messages, and even something specific like "Find a café near my destination."

I can even ask Gemini to find a specific mall or shopping center name from my Google Keep and start navigation. I use voice controls whenever possible because they let me keep my attention where it belongs: on the road.

Small tools that make driving easier

After 10,000 miles with Google Maps, I have realized that the features I value most aren’t necessarily the ones Google puts front and center. Small features like these made a much bigger difference to my everyday driving than I expected. If you spend a lot of time on the road, I recommend enabling and using these Google Maps features.

Waze's planned drives feature solved a problem Google Maps didn't even know I had.

I’ve used VS Code for years, and much of my workflow now lives inside it. I use it for coding, connect it to local AI models, and access my desktop remotely through its tunnel feature. I’ve also tried other editors, including Zed, but VSCodium interests me because it lets me keep the VS Code environment without Microsoft’s telemetry.

The only complication is extensions. You’d expect an editor built from the same source code to support the tools you already use, but VSCodium connects to a different extension registry. The familiar extension panel searches Open VSX instead of Microsoft’s marketplace, and the two don’t offer the same catalog.

Most of the editor comes with me

Some key features don't

VSCodium keeps the parts of VS Code I’m already comfortable with. The file explorer, command palette, split editor, and integrated terminal are all there, along with Git integration for reviewing changes and managing commits. I don’t have to learn new shortcuts or figure out where familiar controls have moved. You can also copy your settings.json and keybindings.json files across, so your preferred editor settings and custom shortcuts can come with you.

There’s a useful distinction between VS Code’s source code and the application Microsoft distributes. The source is MIT-licensed, but Microsoft’s downloadable build includes its own customizations and uses a separate license. VSCodium builds that open-source code into an application with Microsoft’s branding removed and telemetry disabled. You get a ready-made download that’s available on Windows, macOS, and Linux.

VSCodium keeps most things the same as VS Code, but some gaps remain. Beyond extensions, VSCodium also lacks some features available in VS Code. For example, VSCodium doesn't include the Tunnels feature, which is useful if you want to turn your desktop PC into a server you can access from your laptop.

You can still use features like Remote SSH from the integrated terminal, but editing a remote folder through the editor requires an extension. Microsoft’s Remote SSH extension isn’t officially supported in VSCodium, which recommends Open Remote SSH as an alternative. That gives you a way to work on a remote server, though it isn't quite the same setup as Microsoft's extension.

They need to publish it there separately, even if the extension itself works in both editors.

Microsoft restricts its marketplace offerings to Visual Studio products and services, so VSCodium uses an independent registry. Open VSX offers plenty of familiar tools, including Prettier for formatting code, ESLint for checking JavaScript, and Continue and Cline for AI coding assistance.

However, it does lack tools like Microsoft’s C/C++ extension, Live Share for collaborative editing, and its Remote Development extensions. Pylance, which provides Python language support in VS Code, also restricts use in unofficial builds.

You do have alternatives. VSCodium recommends clangd for C/C++ language support, Native Debug for debugging, BasedPyright for Python analysis, and Open Remote SSH and Open Remote WSL for remote development. But whether you can use these alternatives depends on the features available and whether they suit your use case. I was able to replace almost all the extensions I was missing, but it took effort and required some digging.

If an extension isn’t on Open VSX, you can check whether its developer provides a VSIX file on GitHub or another official release page. I rebuilt my VS Code setup from scratch this year, and it's the fastest it's ever been

item.title: One of Wi-Fi 7's best features can actually slow your connection down
item.itunes:title: One of Wi-Fi 7's best features can actually slow your connection down
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Wi-Fi 7 routers came with some new configuration options, and one of the more interesting ones is Multi-Link Operation, or MLO. MLO lets your devices use more than one Wi-Fi band at the same time, and it's one of the biggest reasons why Wi-Fi 7 speeds look so more like a generational leap than the versions before it. It also happens to be one of the first settings I make sure is turned off on a new router. On the more affordable Wi-Fi 7 models and in a house full of older devices, it can do more harm than good.

6 myths you probably still believe about mesh networking

If you've been on the fence about getting a mesh network, or you're set on getting one, make sure you have all the details first.

5
By  Adam Conway

What MLO is and what it's supposed to do

It sounds great on paper

Credit: TP-Link

Until Wi-Fi 7, a phone or laptop talked to the router on one band at a time. Even a tri-band router gave each device a single lane, whether that was 2.4GHz, 5GHz, or 6GHz. If that band got crowded, or you walked out of its range, the device had to drop it and reconnect on another. MLO removes that limit, so that a Wi-Fi 7-enabled device can hold links to the router on multiple bands at a time, and treat those links as a single connection.

This, in theory, delivers more speed, lower latency, and a connection that's more stable than one that relies on just a single link at a time. Both ends of the connection need to support it in order for it to work properly.

MLO also comes in two main modes: STR and eMLSR. In STR mode, a device uses its links at the same time, which is what MLO is usually described as in marketing material. eMLSR works a bit differently, only allowing the device to listen on several bands but only using one to send and receive at a time. This can make a connection feel more stable, but it doesn't make it faster.

Mesh Wi-Fi is causing the exact problems it promised to solve

Why does my home still have dead zones?

19
By  Jasmine Mannan

Many devices can't use more than one link at a time

Even if they advertise Wi-Fi 7 support

The switching mode needs less power, so it's what a lot of client devices ship with. Intel's BE200, a very common laptop card, does show Wi-Fi 7 support in its spec table, but it uses eMLSR across 2.4GHz and 5GHz bands, so the speed boost isn't available there. A lot of other devices fall into that same boat, so turning on MLO is useless in those cases.

Even if your router and devices both support MLO, the network can deliver lower real-world speeds than if you just used single-band 5GHz or 6GHz connection from the same router. TP-Link's own support documentation confirms this, noting that a single band may perform better when a device's MLO support is partial.

Your Wi-Fi isn't slow because of bandwidth — it's because of airtime

Most people never optimize their router's QoS settings

15
By  Tanveer Singh

A dual-band router is rarely worth bonding

It shows its best with 5GHz and 6GHz

MLO is at its best when it pairs 5GHz with 6GHz, two fast bands with room to spare. A dual-band Wi-Fi 7 router doesn't have a 6GHz radio, so the only pairing on offer is 5GHz and 2.4GHz, the slowest and usually the most crowded band in the house. Combining these using MLO is usually just a glorified form of band steering, which is something that almost all modern routers have these days and enables your router to move devices between its bands under one network name.

Wi-Fi 7 is getting cheaper but you still don't need it (for now)
By  Rich Edmonds

It adds friction with older devices

If your house is full of older stuff, MLO can actively inhibit connections

A downstream effect of MLO is how the network gets secured. When 6GHz is part of the link, WPA3 becomes a requirement, and most routers will warn you when you turn it on that you might be cutting off some legacy devices. If you plan on mixing and matching Wi-Fi 7 devices and older hardware, there is a mixed WPA2 and WPA3 mode, but your mileage may vary there, too, because not all devices support that either. MLO also creates another network name in some cases, which adds more friction if you change the name.

3 reasons I'm excited about Wi-Fi 7 in 2025

Wi-Fi 7 is entering its second year, and for those of us with a bevy of connected devices, I'm convinced it's finally time to take it for a spin.

4
By  Andre Revilla

MLO can push great speeds in scenarios where it's suited

It earns its spot in some circumstances

In a mesh system where all of your devices are up-to-date, MLO can be a game changer. Mesh nodes specifically benefit, and the speeds between the nodes can hit multi-gigabit speeds in some cases. If Ethernet isn't an option between your mesh nodes and MLO is supported, it's absolutely worth trying. The same goes for tri-band routers: when paired with devices that can leverage STR, which are admittedly few, speeds can be well above what a single-band connection can offer. Even if eMLSR is the only option, switching between bands in a crowded airspace can ensure your device is sitting on the most optimal band at any given moment.

Wi-Fi 7 routers are finally here, but most homes aren't wired well enough to take advantage

Your home is probably not ready for Wi-Fi 7, and won't be for a long time

13
By  Tanveer Singh

MLO is best skipped unless all of your important devices can handle it

So on a new dual-band router, I'd leave MLO off. On a tri-band router where your mesh nodes or other devices can actually harness it, it's worth at least trying out. As is always the case with wireless networking, real-world results will vary heavily depending on your environment. The construction of your walls and floors, along with other devices in your area and on the network play a massive role in connection quality and speed.

Some would argue that "mid-range" is strictly related to the "tiers" of the chips in the system and where they sit in the product hierarchy, some relate it to an output resolution, most commonly 1440p. And then finally, there's the economic argument, which is the most widely referenced among OEMs, stating that a mid-range PC is one that delivers maximum performance against its price.

The past year has seen some rather unprecedented shifts in the PC hardware economy, largely due to the rising demand from the hyperscalers and AI industry, and the place where it's most pronounced is in DRAM pricing.

The crisis has persisted for so long now that the very notion of what it means to have a mid-range PC has been altered, perhaps permanently. This has also led to a rare inversion in hardware economics, in that, a depreciating asset like my workstation from 2023 has appreciated in its value in fall 2026. Curious to know exactly by how much, I did the math myself.

My PC from 2023 is worth more now than when I built it

The cost accounting has changed, but bookkeepers didn't get the memo

In every bookkeeping framework I have come across, computing hardware is classed as a depreciating asset, because a PC loses performance headroom relative to what's being released, the warranty windows closing, and the resale market thinning out as newer parts arrive on the market.

Three years, going by that framework, is usually enough to knock a mid-range build down to a fraction of its retail price, and that is exactly the trajectory that my PC was on until the beginning of the DRAM crisis.

If you've been keeping up with the news, or if you have been in the market for a new PC, you'll know that this trajectory of depreciation over time has seen a reversal. This isn't something entirely new, since it has happened in the PC DRAM market between 2016 and 2018 under the first wave of hyperscaler data center buildouts, and the GPU market between 2020 and 2022 due to the COVID-19 supply shortage and crypto boom.

Not all components inside the case have uniformly appreciated, though. The motherboard, CPU, the NZXT AIO cooling unit, and the PSU are all worth less, but the increase comes from three parts that are all caught in the same supply crunch, including the DDR5 memory, the GPU, and most recently, my PCIe Gen 4 NVMe SSD.

I've lived through hardware shortages before — this one feels unprecedented

Prepare yourselves for a new normal in pricing and availability

7
By  Tanveer Singh

The 32GB of DDR5 accounts for most of it

It's all about constrained supply and increased demand

I dug up through my Amazon invoices from 2023 to work out exactly what I had paid for this PC, and DDR5 prices felt like they belonged to an alternative reality where the data centers didn't leave consumer computing for dead.

In September 2023, I paid £118.99 (about $157.20) for 32GB of Corsair Vengeance DDR5-6000 CL30 AMD EXPO memory. Today, the exact same SKU is listed at £529.99 (about $700) at Scan.co.uk. Best Buy in the US has it listed at $549.99 at the time of writing.

On average, the same SKU with the same specs sells for around $475, including open-box and refurbished listings. Even the cheapest open-box kit I could find on offer costs roughly thrice as much as what I paid for a sealed, retail-boxed unit.

It's worth qualifying here that I bought my MSI RTX 4070 Ti Super a little later in January 2024 close to its MSRP of $799 which replaced my aging RTX 2070 Super. It's hard to find a new one retailing right now, especially since the Ada Lovelace GPUs have been superseded by the Blackwell series.

The RAM crisis genuinely made cloud gaming look like a better deal

By  Abhinav Raj

My PC is worth more than it was before, and that's horrible news

Whenever an asset that's owned appreciates in value, it's usually good news for the consumer, but that's something I'd argue does not apply to PC hardware. The natural cycle of components is such that they are supposed to depreciate with time, and newer, more performant and competitive products take their place, ideally at a sustainable price in the market.

item.itunes:title: I gave a coding agent my old Bash scripts, and it turned them into one tool I actually use
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I have a bunch of Bash scripts that help me keep my files organized. They’re useful enough that I keep using them, although running everything through the terminal gets cumbersome. I have to keep track of which script does what, remember the commands, and pass the right folder paths and options. I’d much rather open a page, select what I want to do, and click a button.

So I gave Claude Code my existing scripts and asked it to build a basic interface around them. I call it File Manager’s Manager. It’s a simple web page that runs locally on my Mac, giving me one place to run these scripts, choose folders, and see the results.

Putting my scripts to good use

Old scripts make interesting tools

The scripts I gave Claude do a bunch of jobs that are generally tedious for me to do through the file manager. My favorite is a download-cleaner script that sorts files into folders for documents, images, videos, archives, and installers. On top of that, I have a broader folder organizer that does something similar for any folder I point it at, including camera dumps and external drives. All of this is only useful if I know what to expect from the file itself, and the bulk renamer script handles that by replacing filenames like IMG_4928.jpg with a date, prefix, or numbered sequence.

Then there are the scripts I use to find things. The large-file finder lists the biggest files first, and the old-file finder flags files I haven’t modified in a long time. My duplicate finder compares file hashes to identify identical copies, even when their names differ. These give me results to review before I delete anything. Finally, the backup script copies important folders to another location and transfers only new or changed files.

I keep these scripts in a folder and try to remember what each one does, but Claude Code helped me turn them into a single tool. It doesn’t have to be just these scripts; you can do the same with scripts you use to resize images, compress videos, or convert documents.

For example, I use OpenAI’s Whisper to transcribe meetings through the terminal, with separate scripts for languages such as English, Hindi, and Arabic. I’m planning to use Claude Code to build a small interface with a recording selector, a language menu, and other relevant options to make this setup much easier to use.

I connected Claude to my terminal, and now it does things I used to script by hand

Claude replaced my entire scripting workflow

8
By  Anurag Singh

Claude Code built me File Manager’s Manager

And it makes managing files so much easier

I asked Claude Code to put all seven scripts on a single page, with a button for each one. The page runs locally on my Mac and opens in the browser, so I no longer have to remember script names or type commands every time I want to use one. Claude also built the controls around what each script needs. The large-file finder lets me choose a folder and set a minimum file size. The bulk renamer gives me options for prefixes and numbering, and the backup tool just needs a source and destination. When I run something, the page passes those options to the relevant Bash script and shows me the result.

I also asked Claude to add previews anywhere a script could make a mess. If I am renaming hundreds of files, I want to see the old and new names before anything changes. The same goes for the folder organizer, which shows where files are going before moving them. Errors also stay inside the interface. If a backup drive is disconnected or a folder cannot be accessed, I see that on the page instead of having to dig through Terminal output.

Claude Code makes it easier to build tools

You don't need to be a developer

I used Claude Code with Opus 5.5 to build the interface, and it barely took ten minutes. Having the scripts already available gave it something concrete to work with. I could explain how I wanted to use them and let Claude handle the code needed for the page.

Claude Code can read files in your project, make changes across multiple files, and run commands to check its work. For a project like this, it can inspect the scripts to understand which arguments they accept and what they return, then build the controls around those details. You don’t have to manually paste every script into a chat and copy the generated code back into separate files.

You can also keep changing the project through the same conversation. If the rename preview needs another column, or you want a different folder-organization option, you can ask Claude to edit the implementation. When something fails, you can give it the error and ask it to investigate the relevant files.

Make the most out of Claude Code

This is the kind of project I want to use Claude Code for more often. I already have scripts that do useful work, and building an interface around them is something I’d otherwise have to learn and put together myself. You can get more from Claude Code by making a few changes here and there. I’ve seen better output by setting a clear goal for Claude and being precise with my prompt from the start. There are also several settings you can change to make Claude work more efficiently.
